meta.title: Who really said "Eureka! I have found it!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Archimedes never wrote it down. The bath story comes from Vitruvius, two centuries later — and “I have found it” is just what “Eureka” means.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Eureka! I have found it!'?
meta.ogDescription: The earliest account was written 200 years late. And the famous English tag is really what translators add to explain the Greek.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 287 – c. 212 BC · Greek mathematician, physicist & engineer of Syracuse
answer.sourceLine: The bath story is first recorded by the Roman architect Vitruvius, De architectura, Book IX, preface — written in the first century BC, roughly two centuries after Archimedes died. Vitruvius reports a single Greek word, εὕρηκα, shouted twice; nothing in Archimedes’ own surviving writings mentions the episode, and the familiar English tag “I have found it!” is simply what translators add to gloss Eureka.

source.heading: The earliest ancient source

docMeta.dd: De architectura (The Ten Books on Architecture), Book IX, preface
Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, Roman architect — not Archimedes
First century BC — roughly two centuries after Archimedes’ death (c. 212 BC)
Joseph Gwilt (London: Priestley and Weale, 1826); also Morris Hicky Morgan (Harvard University Press, 1914)

source.excerpt: … he immediately followed it up, leapt out of the vessel in joy, and, returning home naked, cried out with a loud voice that he had found that of which he was in search, for he continued exclaiming, in Greek, εὑρηκα, (I have found it out).
trail: First century BC — the earliest surviving witness. The story appears in Vitruvius’s De architectura, Book IX, preface: King Hiero suspects his goldsmith has cut a votive crown with silver, Archimedes solves it in the bath, and runs home shouting. The Latin reads Nam currens identidem graecè clamabat Eurica, Eurica — one word, repeated, as reproduced with the Morgan translation on Chris Rorres’s Archimedes source pages, hosted at NYU ↗. Vitruvius is the earliest account, not the only one: Wikipedia notes ↗ that the story “is told again a century later by Plutarch, though in a shortened version” — which only pushes the first telling further from the man.

The gap nobody can close. Archimedes died around 212 BC. Scientific American ↗ dates the telling: “The oldest authority for the naked-Archimedes eureka story is Vitruvius, a Roman writer, who included the tale in his introduction to his ninth book of architecture some time in the first century B.C.” That is roughly two centuries of silence between the bath and the first surviving word about it.

Archimedes never mentions it. Scientific American’s “Fact or Fiction?” ↗ notes that Archimedes himself never wrote about the episode, though he documented a great deal else, and quotes mathematician Chris Rorres on the displacement method: it “works in theory so it sounds right but when you actually try it you find that the real world gets in the way.”

Where the reference works land. Wikiquote ↗ carries it in its main quotes section — not under Misattributed — sourced to “Vitruvius Pollio in De Architectura, ix.215,” and glosses εὕρηκα as “I have found it! or I have got it!, commonly quoted as Eureka!” — the gloss and the exclamation presented as the same thing, which is exactly the point.
source.excerptNote: Look closely at what is inside the parentheses. “I have found it out” is Gwilt’s translation of the Greek word immediately before it — a footnote for readers who don’t read Greek, not a second sentence Archimedes shouted. Morgan’s 1914 version, as reproduced on Chris Rorres’s Archimedes pages, renders the same moment as the Greek doubled: “Εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα.”

source.rightsNote: Vitruvius wrote in the first century BC, so the underlying text is long out of copyright, and rights here turn on the translation you quote. Both standard English versions that carry this passage predate 1931 and are public domain in the US: Joseph Gwilt’s (London: Priestley and Weale, 1826), reproduced at LacusCurtius ↗, and Morris Hicky Morgan’s (Harvard University Press, 1914), which Project Gutenberg ↗ hosts in full. A post-1931 translation of the same passage would be a different matter.

author.name: Archimedes
author.heading: The man who really did discover it
author.metaLine: c. 287 – c. 212 BC · Greek mathematician, physicist & engineer of Syracuse
author.bio: Archimedes of Syracuse was the ancient world’s most formidable mathematician — he pinned down π between useful bounds, worked out the law of the lever, and founded the study of hydrostatics, the science of bodies in fluid — though the bath story as Vitruvius tells it turns on measuring displaced volume, not on the buoyancy principle that carries his name. A substantial body of his own writing survives, including On Floating Bodies, and it is meticulous, formal, and entirely silent about crowns, baths, and running naked through Syracuse. Almost everything colourful we ‘know’ about him — the bath, the burning mirrors, the death at a Roman sword while drawing figures in the sand — reaches us from writers working centuries after his death.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the famous version
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual. The quote isn’t pinned on the wrong person — an ancient source really does put it in Archimedes’ mouth. The problem is subtler, and there are three layers of it.

items.who: A translator’s gloss, read as a second exclamation
items.why: Eureka — εὕρηκα — means “I have found it.” It is the first-person perfect of the Greek verb ‘to find’, as Wikipedia sets out ↗. You can see the redundancy being born in Gwilt’s 1826 translation, which prints the English in parentheses as a gloss on the Greek immediately before it: “εὑρηκα, (I have found it out)” — a note for readers without Greek, not a second thing Archimedes shouted. Exactly how that gloss hardened into the popular doubled tag isn’t documented; what is certain is that “Eureka! I have found it!” says the same thing twice, in two languages.

No contemporary of Archimedes records the bath, the crown, or the shout. The earliest surviving account is Vitruvius’s, and Scientific American ↗ notes that Archimedes never wrote about the episode himself — leaving two centuries in which a good story could be improved in the telling.

items.who: Doubted by scientists from Galileo onward
items.why: Even if he said it, the water-displacement test as Vitruvius describes it may not be what he actually did. Scholars have objected ↗ that an adulterated crown would displace only a minutely different volume of water — a difference the instruments of the day could not reliably measure.

misattribution.truthLine: The likeliest truth: Archimedes really did crack hydrostatics, and he wrote the real proof down himself in On Floating Bodies — no bathtub required. The shout is Vitruvius’s, two centuries after the fact, and it was only ever one word. Read the passage yourself ↗ and you’ll see the second half of the famous quote sitting quietly inside a translator’s parentheses.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: It is the most famous exclamation in the history of science, and it is a single word — a word that already contains its own translation. Every time someone writes “Eureka! I have found it!” they are saying it twice: once in Greek, once in the English that translators supply to explain the Greek.

That’s a small joke, but it points at something real. The Archimedes we quote is almost entirely a literary character assembled by Romans and Greeks writing generations after his death — the bath, the burning mirrors, the last words in the sand. The Archimedes who actually existed left behind something far better than an exclamation: rigorous proofs, in his own hand, that still hold. On Floating Bodies needs no anecdote to be astonishing.
context.detailsSummary: So what did the crown test actually involve?
detailsBody: Vitruvius describes a volume comparison: take a mass of pure gold and a mass of pure silver, each weighing the same as the crown, and measure how much water each displaces. Then measure the crown. If it displaces more than the gold, it isn’t pure gold. The logic is sound and the arithmetic works.

The trouble is engineering, not maths. A votive crown is not large, an adulterated one displaces only a hair more water than a pure one, and surface tension alone can swamp the difference. Galileo doubted the account, and mathematician Chris Rorres put the modern objection compactly to Scientific American ↗: the volumetric method “works in theory so it sounds right but when you actually try it you find that the real world gets in the way.” A balance scale weighing the crown against gold while both were submerged would have been far more practical — and rather more like the Archimedes of the surviving treatises.
context.pull: “Eureka” already means “I have found it.” The famous quote is one word and its own footnote, holding hands.
